lines.text: Your phone knows where you are within a few meters. But it never tells the satellites anything. It only listens.
About thirty GPS satellites circle the Earth, twenty thousand kilometers up. Each one carries atomic clocks.
Every satellite keeps shouting the same thing: who it is, where it is, and the exact time, down to billionths of a second.
Those signals travel at the speed of light, but even light takes a moment to get here. About a fifteenth of a second.
So your phone checks how late each message arrives. The delay tells it how far away that satellite is.
One satellite puts you somewhere on a giant sphere. Two narrow it to a circle. Three, to just a couple of points.
And a fourth fixes your phone's own clock, because your phone doesn't have an atomic clock. Now it knows exactly where you are.
Here's the wild part. Up there, clocks tick slightly faster, thanks to Einstein's relativity. About thirty-eight millionths of a second a day.
Sounds tiny. But if nobody corrected it, GPS would drift by about ten kilometers every single day.
GPS finds you. Orbi Transfer lets your team find each other's files, without sharing anyone's location. A private Space, locked with a passcode.
